title: Philip K. Dick's Paranoia (MA Thesis)
author: David Gill
card_summary: David Gill's 2006 master's thesis on PKD's paranoia, structured in two chapters — 'Time Out of Joint' (the 1959 novel as the inaugural staging of PKD's ontological-paranoid problem) and 'Dick's Paranoia' (the November 1971 break-in and its aftermath as the biographical key, read through Freudian and clinical literature on paranoia). Predates Gill's Total Dick-Head blog (launched 2007) and the Exegesis publication (2011) and grounds the methodological frame Gill carries into his later public-facing work.
page_summary:
David Gill's 2006 master's thesis is the textual foundation of his subsequent fan-academic career on Philip K. Dick. Working before the 2011 publication of the Exegesis and before the launch of the Total Dick-Head blog (2007), Gill builds a sustained reading of PKD's paranoia as both literary structure and biographical fact across two chapters. The introduction stages the thesis through two anchor incidents — the late-1950s bathroom light-cord moment (which, per Sutin, becomes the seed of Time Out of Joint) and the November 17, 1971 San Rafael break-in (which Gill treats as the load-bearing biographical event for understanding PKD's late-period speculation).

Chapter One reads Time Out of Joint (1959) as the inaugural staging of PKD's signature ontological-paranoid problem: an insignificant protagonist (Ragle Gumm) discovers that his reality is a constructed illusion designed to keep him from recognizing his own load-bearing significance. Gill traces the structure across PKD's earlier 1950s commercial fiction and shows how Time Out of Joint formalizes a problem the genre had only gestured at.

Chapter Two ('Dick's Paranoia') reads the November 1971 break-in through the clinical and Freudian literature on paranoia (Freud's Schreber case, Martin Kantor's Understanding Paranoia, Swanson-Bohnert-Smith's The Paranoid). Gill's approach is to take PKD's paranoid theorizing seriously as both pathology and as productive cognitive operation — a frame that anticipates Kyle Arnold's 2016 psychobiographical reading from a different angle. The chapter integrates Sutin's biographical reconstruction (1989), Anne Dick's contestation (1995), Carrère's I Am Alive and You Are Dead (2004), and the Sonic Youth reception via Foege's Confusion is Next (1994) as part of a broader cultural account of how PKD's paranoia has been received.

Contributions to PKD studies: (1) the textual foundation of David Gill's subsequent career as a public-facing PKD scholar (Total Dick-Head blog, SF State Dick-Fest, Exegesis annotations); (2) one of the more disciplined treatments of the November 1971 break-in in academic Dick scholarship; (3) integration of clinical paranoia literature into Dick studies in a way later anticipated by Arnold (2016); (4) early academic recognition of PKD's reception in contemporary American music (Sonic Youth) as part of his cultural afterlife.

Works Cited: Carrère's I Am Alive and You Are Dead (2004), Sutin's Divine Invasions (1989), Robinson's The Novels of Philip K. Dick (1984), Mackey's Twayne PKD (1988), Warrick's Mind in Motion (1987), Suvin's 'Artifice as Refuge and World View' (1983), Krabbenhoft's 'Uses of Madness in Cervantes and Philip K. Dick' (SFS 2000), Foege's Confusion is Next (1994), Williams's Rolling Stone profile (1975), and the clinical paranoia literature.

Position in the literature: a master's thesis rather than a published monograph, but a substantive document that grounds Gill's later interventions in the field. Read alongside Arnold's clinical-psychological monograph and Carrère's biographical novel as part of the cluster of paranoia-focused readings.
